original: Communication Rights of ____________. Every person, regardless of the type or severity of disability, holds fundamental rights related to communication. Basic rights: the right to services that improve communication; the right to communicate using spoken language; the right to communicate using nonverbal and augmentative means. Choice: the right to make choices; the right to request desired objects, actions, events, and people; the right to refuse undesired objects, actions, events, and people. Expression: the right to express feelings; the right to share opinions and ideas; the right to ask and answer questions. Social participation: the right to social interaction; the right to communication that is relevant to one's interests; the right to receive information about the people and events in one's environment. Community: the right to communicate across different settings; the right to inclusion in the community; the right to communication consistent with one's cultural and linguistic background. Communication partners: the right to receive a response; the right to be treated with dignity and respect; the right to be addressed directly rather than spoken about. These rights apply to all individuals.

source: Neuroplasticity patient education (adapted from Kleim & Jones, 2008, JSLHR 51)
original: Principles of Experience-Dependent Neuroplasticity: Patient Education. The brain can reorganize to improve cognitive function, but this change depends on active engagement. (1) Use it or lose it: cognitive domains include reasoning, memory, auditory comprehension, attention, and language. Domains that are engaged are strengthened; domains that are not engaged deteriorate. (2) Use it and improve it: improving a specific skill requires training that skill. Tasks should be challenging but achievable. (3) Specificity: choose novel, creative, and active rather than passive activities. A passive activity can be made active, for example by recording points, fouls, and time-outs while watching a basketball game. Recommended activities: keeping a journal (thoughts, goals, memories); keeping lists (plans, tasks, groceries); games (crossword, Sudoku, riddles, puzzles, Scrabble, Pictionary, Taboo, Mad Libs, cards); internet research (look up a person and record their history, research personal interests, learn a new craft or project). (4) Repetition: daily practice is required. For example, improving writing requires writing daily; writing on only 1 or 2 days is not sufficient. (5) Intensity: increased effort and time increase skill gains; meaningful change requires many hours of practice. (6) Time: begin now. The brain continues to change over a long period. (7) Salience: activities that are personally meaningful produce greater improvement. Social engagement is recommended: time with family or friends, attending church, community volunteering, and a genuine conversation every day. Patient plan: ____________.

target.title: Tips to keep your brain healthy

original: Home Exercise Program: Independent Communication Practice. The following activities support progress toward communication goals. Verbal expression: oral reading daily, repeating passages until fluent; functional scripts (write down frequently used phrases and rehearse until automatic); loudness monitoring with the Noise Meter Pro app for visual feedback on vocal loudness; confrontation naming of objects or people in the home, in magazines, or in photographs, creating a practice set, repeating it, and describing each item named. Reading comprehension: audiobooks, reading along while listening, or reading a passage independently and then listening to verify comprehension (sources: Audible reading app; BARD website, free audiobooks; LibriVox website, free audiobooks); eBooks with enlarged text and increased white space. Written expression: speech-to-text on a phone or tablet (speak the word, copy it, use it to verify spelling); texting or email, one message daily, using spell check and word prediction, and text-to-speech if stuck; Scrabble tiles (copy letters, build words, check spelling on a phone); copy and recall (copy written text such as birthday cards, greeting cards, books, emails, or texts, then attempt to write the message without looking). Auditory comprehension: podcasts (recall important details, sequence events, add a second task for challenge); listening to television without watching (record sports scores, follow soap opera plots, check understanding by watching). Conversational strategies: prepare for conversations in advance by taking photos of people or activities, creating photo albums, writing scripts on likely topics, and bringing pen and paper. You are in charge of your recovery: set personal goals and challenge yourself.

original: Accidente cerebrovascular (derrame cerebral): información para pacientes. Un accidente cerebrovascular, también llamado "ataque cerebral", ocurre cuando se interrumpe la circulación de sangre en el cerebro. Esto sucede por la obstrucción de un vaso sanguíneo en el cerebro o el cuello (accidente isquémico), o por la ruptura de un vaso con sangrado dentro del cerebro (accidente hemorrágico). Cualquier persona puede tener un derrame cerebral. Ciertos factores de riesgo aumentan la posibilidad: edad, género, raza, antecedentes familiares de derrame cerebral, presión arterial alta, obesidad, falta de ejercicio, diabetes, enfermedad del corazón (cardiopatía), desequilibrio del colesterol y fumar cigarrillos. Los factores de riesgo que usted puede controlar son: la presión arterial alta, la obesidad, la diabetes, la cardiopatía, el desequilibrio del colesterol, fumar cigarrillos y la falta de ejercicio. Consulte a su médico para aprender cómo controlarlos. Para prevenir un derrame cerebral: visite al médico con regularidad, tome sus medicamentos como se le recetaron, deje de fumar y haga ejercicio con frecuencia. Conozca los síntomas con la palabra HEROE: H, habla incoherente o extraña; E, extremidades con parálisis, adormecimiento o debilidad; R, rostro adormecido o desviado; O, ojo cegado o paralizado; E, emergencia. Si tiene estos síntomas, llame al 911.

source: Pairing hearing aids with iPhone (based on Apple support instructions)
original: Pairing Made for iPhone Hearing Aids. Pairing your hearing aids with your iPhone can improve audibility for phone calls and for speech practice activities. Instructions: 1. Open the battery doors on your hearing aids. 2. Unlock your iPhone. 3. Go to Settings. 4. Select General. 5. Select Accessibility. 6. Select Hearing Aids. 7. Close the battery doors on your hearing aids. 8. When the name of your hearing aids appears, tap it. 9. Tap "Pair" when the pairing request appears. 10. Wait; pairing can take up to one minute. 11. Confirm the pairing: a check mark appears next to the hearing aid name, and hearing aid controls are available on the Lock Screen.
